questions.title: Customer Order Analysis

questions.title: Latest Two Payments Per Customer
questions.intro: Each row in payments represents a separate payment. A customer can have more than two payments or only one payment, and multiple payments can happen on the same date.
task: Find the two most recent payments for each customer using ROW_NUMBER() and a CTE (WITH clause).

    SELECT payment_id, customer_id, payment_date, amount,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
               PARTITION BY customer_id
               ORDER BY payment_date DESC, payment_id DESC
           ) AS rn
    FROM payments
)

FROM ranked_payments
WHERE rn <= 2
ORDER BY customer_id ASC, payment_date DESC, payment_id DESC;

The outer query keeps row numbers 1 and 2, removes the rn column from display, and sorts the remaining seven rows in the requested order.

questions.title: Daily Paid Revenue Running Total
questions.intro: A sales platform records purchases at different stores. Multiple paid purchases can occur at the same store on the same date. Failed and Refunded purchases do not count toward revenue.
task: Use a CTE to calculate daily_revenue as the sum of amounts for Paid sales on each store_id and sale_date.

    SELECT store_id, sale_date, SUM(amount) AS daily_revenue

questions.title: Weekly Revenue Change Using LAG
questions.intro: A retailer stores individual sales transactions. Compute each store's total completed revenue for each recorded week and compare it with the previous week that had completed sales.
task: Use a CTE (WITH clause) to calculate weekly_revenue = SUM(amount) for only Completed sales, grouped by store_id and week_start.

Using LAG() OVER (PARTITION BY store_id ORDER BY week_start), calculate previous_revenue from the previous RECORDED week with completed sales for the same store (not necessarily the immediately preceding calendar week).
Calculate revenue_change = weekly_revenue - previous_revenue. For a store's first recorded completed-sales week, both previous_revenue and revenue_change must be NULL.
Exclude weeks with zero Completed sales; exclude stores with no Completed sales.
Display store_id, week_start, weekly_revenue, previous_revenue, revenue_change, and order by store_id ascending and week_start ascending.
questions.note: NULL values in the expected output are SQL NULL values, not the text 'NULL'. Store 2 has no Completed sales in the week of 2026-10-12, so the 2026-10-19 row compares to 2026-10-05.
questions.hint: Aggregate first, then apply LAG to the aggregated rows—not to individual transactions. You can use a second CTE so that revenue_change can reuse the previous_revenue alias.
questions.solution:
WITH weekly_sales AS (
    SELECT store_id, week_start, SUM(amount) AS weekly_revenue
    FROM sales
    WHERE status = 'Completed'
    GROUP BY store_id, week_start
), weekly_with_previous AS (
    SELECT store_id,
           week_start,
           weekly_revenue,
           LAG(weekly_revenue) OVER (
               PARTITION BY store_id
               ORDER BY week_start
           ) AS previous_revenue
    FROM weekly_sales
)
SELECT store_id,
       week_start,
       weekly_revenue,
       previous_revenue,
       weekly_revenue - previous_revenue AS revenue_change
FROM weekly_with_previous
ORDER BY store_id ASC, week_start ASC;

For store 2, the Refunded-only 2026-10-12 week is absent. The 2026-10-19 row therefore compares its 650 against 700 from 2026-10-05.

questions.solution:
WITH rolling AS (
    SELECT sensor_id, reading_id, recorded_at,
           AVG(temperature) OVER (
               PARTITION BY sensor_id
               ORDER BY recorded_at, reading_id
               ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
           ) AS rolling_avg,
           COUNT(*) OVER (
               PARTITION BY sensor_id
               ORDER BY recorded_at, reading_id
               ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
           ) AS window_count
    FROM sensor_readings
)
SELECT sensor_id, reading_id, recorded_at,
       ROUND(rolling_avg, 2) AS avg_last_three
FROM rolling
WHERE window_count = 3
ORDER BY sensor_id, recorded_at, reading_id;
steps: PARTITION BY sensor_id keeps each sensor's readings independent. Within each partition, recorded_at and reading_id determine the chronological order even when timestamps match.
Sensor A's ordered temperatures are 20, 22, 24, 26 and 31. Sensor B's are 30, 33, 36 and 39. Sensor C has only one reading.
The ROWS frame contains at most three physical rows: the current row and two earlier rows. AVG computes their mean and COUNT tells us whether the frame is complete.
The outer WHERE keeps only rows with a frame count of three. This removes the first two readings of A and B and the sole reading of C. ROUND and ORDER BY format and sort the remaining five rows.

checks.error: Calculate an average temperature.
Keep each sensor's readings separate.
Use a three-row window ending at the current reading.
Round the result to two decimal places.
Use the requested output alias.

questions.title: Employees Earning More Than Their Manager
questions.intro: The employees table stores one row per employee. employee_id is the primary key; manager_id references the employee_id of the employee's immediate manager, or is NULL for employees without a manager. Salaries are non-NULL monthly amounts. Find employees whose salary exceeds their immediate manager's salary.
task: Use a self JOIN of employees to match each employee with their immediate manager using manager_id and employee_id.
Include only employees earning strictly more than their immediate manager. Exclude employees without a manager and those earning exactly the same amount as their manager.
Display exactly employee_name, manager_name, employee_salary, manager_salary, and salary_difference (employee_salary minus manager_salary).
Sort by salary_difference descending, then employee_name ascending. Employee names in this sample are unique.
questions.hint: Give the same table two different aliases, one for the employee and one for their manager. Compare their salaries after joining.
questions.solution:
SELECT e.employee_name, m.employee_name AS manager_name,
       e.salary AS employee_salary, m.salary AS manager_salary,
       e.salary - m.salary AS salary_difference
FROM employees e
JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.employee_id
WHERE e.salary > m.salary
ORDER BY salary_difference DESC, e.employee_name ASC;
steps: Read employees twice using aliases e (employee) and m (manager).
Match e.manager_id to m.employee_id. For example, Neha has manager_id 3, so her manager is Diya. Employees Meera and Ishaan have no manager, so the INNER JOIN excludes them.
Compare the two salaries. Diya earns less than Meera; Riya earns exactly as much as Arun. Both are excluded.
The remaining employees are Arun, Kabir, Neha, Vikram and Anya. Their salary differences are 5000, 5000, 7000, 5000 and 5000 respectively.
Sort by difference descending, putting Neha first, then alphabetically among the four employees tied at 5000.

questions.title: Project Budget Audit Across Two Cost Tables
questions.intro: A project has a fixed budget and can incur labor costs in work_logs and purchase costs in expenses. Each project can have zero or many rows in either cost table. All costs and budgets are non-NULL, non-negative numeric values. Find projects that have exceeded their budget without counting costs multiple times.
task: Use a single SELECT query with CTEs (WITH) to compute the total labor cost and total expense separately for each project before joining those totals to projects.
Treat missing labor or expense rows as a cost of 0. Projects with no records in one or both cost tables must still be considered.
Return only projects where the combined cost is strictly greater than the budget; projects exactly at budget must not appear.
Display exactly project_name, budget, labor_total, expense_total, total_cost and over_budget (total_cost minus budget).
Sort by over_budget descending, then project_name ascending.
questions.hint: Aggregate the two child tables independently. Joining raw work logs to raw expenses can multiply rows. LEFT JOIN the aggregated results and use COALESCE for missing totals.
questions.solution:
WITH labor AS (
    SELECT project_id, SUM(labor_cost) AS labor_total
    FROM work_logs
    GROUP BY project_id
), purchases AS (
    SELECT project_id, SUM(amount) AS expense_total
    FROM expenses
    GROUP BY project_id
), costs AS (
    SELECT p.project_name, p.budget,
           COALESCE(l.labor_total, 0) AS labor_total,
           COALESCE(e.expense_total, 0) AS expense_total
    FROM projects p
    LEFT JOIN labor l ON l.project_id = p.project_id
    LEFT JOIN purchases e ON e.project_id = p.project_id
)
SELECT project_name, budget, labor_total, expense_total,
       labor_total + expense_total AS total_cost,
       labor_total + expense_total - budget AS over_budget
FROM costs
WHERE labor_total + expense_total > budget
ORDER BY over_budget DESC, project_name ASC;
steps: Atlas has two labor records and two expense records. A direct join of both child tables would produce four combinations and double-count costs.
The labor CTE produces one row per project with labor records: Atlas 700, Beacon 500, Cedar 550 and Flux 200.
The purchases CTE produces one row per project with expenses: Atlas 450, Beacon 300, Delta 750 and Flux 50.
LEFT JOIN the two totals to all six projects. COALESCE converts missing totals to zero, so Delta has zero labor cost, Cedar has zero expense cost, and Echo has zero for both.
Add the totals: Atlas 1150, Beacon 800, Cedar 550, Delta 750, Echo 0 and Flux 250. Compare each to its own budget. Beacon is exactly at budget, so it is excluded along with Echo and Flux.
Atlas and Delta exceed their budget by 150 each, and Cedar by 50. Sort the tied projects alphabetically before Cedar.

questions.title: Median Delivery Time per Carrier
questions.intro: The shipments table records the carrier, shipment status and delivery_days. shipment_id is unique. Delivered shipments always have a non-NULL integer delivery_days. Calculate each carrier's median delivery duration using only Delivered shipments. A median is the middle value of a sorted list with odd length, or the average of the two middle values when the list has even length.
task: Use a CTE with ROW_NUMBER() to assign positions within each carrier, sorted by delivery_days ascending and shipment_id ascending as the tie-breaker.
Use COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY carrier) to determine the number of Delivered shipments per carrier. Filter to status = 'Delivered' before calculating either window function.
For odd counts, choose the one middle row. For even counts, average the two middle rows. Count duplicate delivery durations as separate shipments; do not use DISTINCT.
Display exactly carrier and median_delivery_days, rounded to two decimal places. Exclude carriers with no Delivered shipments.
Sort by median_delivery_days ascending, then carrier ascending.
questions.hint: For n sorted values with positions starting at 1, the middle positions are FLOOR((n+1)/2) and FLOOR((n+2)/2). For odd n the two positions are equal; for even n they differ by one.
questions.solution:
WITH ranked AS (
    SELECT carrier, delivery_days,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
               PARTITION BY carrier
               ORDER BY delivery_days, shipment_id
           ) AS rn,
           COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY carrier) AS n
    FROM shipments
    WHERE status = 'Delivered'
)
SELECT carrier, ROUND(AVG(delivery_days), 2) AS median_delivery_days
FROM ranked
WHERE rn IN (FLOOR((n + 1) / 2), FLOOR((n + 2) / 2))
GROUP BY carrier
ORDER BY median_delivery_days ASC, carrier ASC;
steps: Filter out Cancelled and In Transit shipments first. RoadLink has no Delivered shipments and therefore never enters the CTE.

Swift has five Delivered durations: 2, 4, 4, 7, 9. Assign positions 1 through 5, keeping both shipments with duration 4. Both middle-position formulas equal 3, so only row 3 remains and the median is 4.
ParcelPro has four durations: 2, 3, 6, 8. The middle positions are 2 and 3. Their average is (3 + 6) / 2 = 4.5.
QuickBox has only one Delivered shipment, with duration 5. Both formulas equal position 1, so its median is 5.
GROUP BY carrier averages the selected middle values per carrier. ROUND formats to two decimal places, and ORDER BY sorts Swift, ParcelPro, then QuickBox.

questions.title: Suppliers With Consistent Quality
questions.intro: The supplier_inspections table stores one inspection per inspection_id. Scores are non-NULL integer values from 0 to 100. Only finalized inspections count toward the quality audit.
task: Return suppliers with at least three Finalized inspections, where every Finalized score is at least 80.
Ignore Draft inspections completely, including when computing the minimum and average.
Display exactly supplier_id, inspection_count, minimum_score and average_score (rounded to two decimal places).
Sort by average_score descending, then supplier_id ascending.
questions.hint: Filter finalized rows before grouping. Use HAVING to check both the number of inspections and the minimum score.
questions.solution:
SELECT supplier_id, COUNT(*) AS inspection_count,
       MIN(score) AS minimum_score, ROUND(AVG(score), 2) AS average_score
FROM supplier_inspections
WHERE status = 'Finalized'
GROUP BY supplier_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3 AND MIN(score) >= 80
ORDER BY average_score DESC, supplier_id ASC;
steps: Discard Draft inspections. Supplier 101's score of 30 is a Draft and does not count; supplier 106 has no finalized rows.
Group the remaining rows by supplier_id. Supplier 103 has only two finalized inspections and fails the count condition.
Supplier 102 has three finalized scores, but its minimum is 70, so it fails the quality condition.
Suppliers 101, 104 and 105 pass. Their minimum scores are 85, 80 and 80, and averages are 90, 80 and 90 respectively.
Sort by average descending, then supplier ID ascending to place 101 before 105, followed by 104.

questions.title: Reserve Inventory Without Overselling
questions.intro: Inventory contains one row per product_id. Reservation requests contain unique request IDs and positive integer quantities. A batch job must reserve the total requested quantity of each product, but only when that product has enough available units. Assume this is a one-time operation on the provided snapshot with no concurrent changes.
task: Write exactly one MySQL 8.0 UPDATE statement using a JOIN to a derived table that sums Pending request quantities per product_id.
For each product, if the total Pending quantity is less than or equal to available_qty, subtract the total from available_qty and add the same total to reserved_qty.
If the total exceeds available_qty, leave both inventory columns unchanged; do not partially reserve requests. Products with no Pending requests must also remain unchanged.
Do not modify reservation_requests or hardcode individual product IDs or quantities. The expected output shows the entire inventory table after the UPDATE, ordered by product_id for illustration.
questions.hint: Aggregate Pending requests by product_id inside a subquery in the JOIN, then compare that sum against available_qty in the UPDATE's WHERE clause.
questions.solution:
UPDATE inventory AS i
JOIN (
    SELECT product_id, SUM(quantity) AS pending_qty
    FROM reservation_requests
    WHERE status = 'Pending'
    GROUP BY product_id
) AS r ON r.product_id = i.product_id
SET i.available_qty = i.available_qty - r.pending_qty,
    i.reserved_qty = i.reserved_qty + r.pending_qty
WHERE i.available_qty >= r.pending_qty;
steps: Filter requests to Pending status. Ignore request 13, 17 and 18.
Sum quantities by product: product 1 needs 7, product 2 needs 7, product 3 needs 8, and product 6 needs 1. Products 4 and 5 have no Pending requests.
Join the totals to inventory. Products 2 and 6 lack sufficient stock, so both of their inventory values remain unchanged.
Product 1 has 12 available and 3 reserved. Subtract 7 from available and add 7 to reserved, giving 5 and 10.
Product 3 has exactly 8 available, so reserving 8 is allowed. It ends with 0 available and 8 reserved. Products 4 and 5 remain unchanged because the derived table has no matching rows.

questions.title: Detect New Personal Best Scores
questions.intro: Each row in game_attempts represents one attempt by a player. Scores and played_at values are non-NULL. Multiple attempts can occur at the same timestamp; the lower attempt_id happened first.
task: Use a CTE and MAX(score) as a window function to calculate each attempt's previous_best: the maximum score from all strictly earlier attempts by the same player.
Order attempts within each player by played_at ascending, then attempt_id ascending. Use a ROWS window frame ending at 1 PRECEDING so the current attempt is excluded.
Return only attempts whose score is strictly greater than previous_best. Exclude first attempts (which have no previous best) and scores equal to a previous best.
Display exactly player_id, attempt_id, played_at, score, previous_best and improvement (score minus previous_best).
Sort by player_id ascending, played_at ascending, then attempt_id ascending.
questions.hint: Use MAX(score) OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ... ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING), then filter the calculated value in the outer query.
questions.solution:
WITH attempt_history AS (
    SELECT player_id, attempt_id, played_at, score,
           MAX(score) OVER (
               PARTITION BY player_id
               ORDER BY played_at, attempt_id
               ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING
           ) AS previous_best
    FROM game_attempts
)
SELECT player_id, attempt_id, played_at, score, previous_best,
       score - previous_best AS improvement
FROM attempt_history
WHERE score > previous_best
ORDER BY player_id, played_at, attempt_id;
steps: Order each player's attempts by timestamp and attempt ID. The first attempt has an empty preceding frame, so previous_best is NULL and it is excluded by the WHERE comparison.
Player 101's second attempt scores 40 against the earlier best of 50, so it does not qualify. Attempt 3 scores 60 against a previous best of 50, improving by 10.

Attempt 4 shares the timestamp with attempt 3 but comes later by ID. It ties the previous best of 60, so it is excluded. Attempt 5 scores 55 and is also excluded. Attempt 6 improves the best from 60 to 75, by 15.
Player 102's attempts 8 and 9 do not beat 90. Attempt 10 scores 95, improving by 5. Player 103 has only one attempt, and player 104 never beats the first score.
Return the three qualifying attempts and sort by player, timestamp and attempt ID.

questions.title: Payment Reconciliation Exceptions
questions.intro: The internal_payments table records payments in the application. The processor_payments table records the corresponding payment processor results. Each table has at most one row per payment_id. Amounts are non-NULL integer cents and currencies are non-NULL three-letter codes. Audit internal payments only; processor-only records are outside this audit.
task: Use a LEFT JOIN to compare each internal payment with its processor record using payment_id.
Return only internal payments with no matching processor record, a different amount, or a different currency. Exclude exact matches and processor-only records.

Display exactly payment_id, internal_amount, processor_amount, and issue. Assign issue using CASE: 'Missing' if no processor row exists; otherwise 'Both mismatch' if both amount and currency differ; otherwise 'Amount mismatch' or 'Currency mismatch' as appropriate.
For missing processor records, processor_amount must be NULL. Sort by payment_id ascending.
questions.hint: Keep internal_payments on the left. Test the joined payment_id for NULL before comparing values. In CASE, test the condition for both mismatches before the individual conditions.
questions.solution:
SELECT i.payment_id, i.amount_cents AS internal_amount,
       p.amount_cents AS processor_amount,
       CASE
           WHEN p.payment_id IS NULL THEN 'Missing'
           WHEN i.amount_cents <> p.amount_cents AND i.currency <> p.currency THEN 'Both mismatch'
           WHEN i.amount_cents <> p.amount_cents THEN 'Amount mismatch'
           ELSE 'Currency mismatch'
       END AS issue
FROM internal_payments AS i
LEFT JOIN processor_payments AS p ON p.payment_id = i.payment_id
WHERE p.payment_id IS NULL
   OR i.amount_cents <> p.amount_cents
   OR i.currency <> p.currency
ORDER BY i.payment_id;
steps: LEFT JOIN the processor table to internal payments. IDs 103 and 107 have no processor match, so their processor columns are NULL. ID 108 appears only in the processor and cannot enter the result.
Compare the amounts and currencies of matched records. IDs 101 and 106 match exactly, so WHERE removes them.
ID 102 differs only in amount; ID 104 differs only in currency. ID 105 differs in both amount and currency.
CASE first detects missing records, then both mismatches, then the individual mismatch types. The remaining ELSE is a currency mismatch because WHERE already removed exact matches.
Return the five exception rows in payment_id order. The processor amounts of IDs 103 and 107 remain NULL.

questions.title: Product Price at the Time of Purchase
questions.intro: Each row in purchases records a product and purchase date. product_price_history records the price in cents starting on each effective_from date. A price stays in effect until a newer price takes effect. The pair (product_id, effective_from) is unique. All dates are DATE values and all recorded prices are non-NULL.
task: For every purchase, find the most recent price for its product whose effective_from is on or before purchased_on. A price effective on the purchase date must be eligible.
Use a LEFT JOIN and a correlated scalar subquery with MAX(effective_from) to identify the applicable price date. Do not select a future price.
Keep purchases with no applicable price, including products with no price history. For those purchases, unit_price_cents and total_cents must both be NULL.
Display exactly purchase_id, product_id, unit_price_cents and total_cents (quantity multiplied by the applicable unit price). Sort by purchase_id ascending.
questions.hint: For each purchase, the correlated MAX subquery should filter by the current product_id and effective_from <= purchased_on. Match the history row on both product_id and that returned date, using LEFT JOIN.
questions.solution:
SELECT p.purchase_id, p.product_id,
       h.price_cents AS unit_price_cents,
       p.quantity * h.price_cents AS total_cents
FROM purchases AS p
LEFT JOIN product_price_history AS h
    ON h.product_id = p.product_id
   AND h.effective_from = (
       SELECT MAX(h2.effective_from)
       FROM product_price_history AS h2
       WHERE h2.product_id = p.product_id
         AND h2.effective_from <= p.purchased_on
   )
ORDER BY p.purchase_id;
steps: For purchase 1, product 101 has no price on or before November 1. MAX returns NULL, so the LEFT JOIN preserves the purchase with NULL price and total.

For purchase 2, the eligible dates are November 2 and November 5. MAX chooses November 5, giving 1200 cents. Purchase 3 still uses that price because the November 20 change is in the future; 3 × 1200 = 3600.
For purchases 4 and 5, product 102's October 25 price of 500 applies. Its November 10 price is too late for both purchases. Their totals are 500 and 1000.
Product 103 has no price history, so purchase 6 remains with NULL price and total. Purchase 7 occurs on November 20, when the new 900-cent price takes effect; its total is 1800.
Return all seven purchases in ID order. Because each product and effective date pair is unique, each purchase matches at most one price row.

questions.title: Find All Reports in a Management Hierarchy
questions.intro: The employees table represents an acyclic management hierarchy. employee_id is the unique primary key and manager_id references another employee, or is NULL for a root. Each employee has at most one immediate manager. The organization needs all direct and indirect reports of employee 10, grouped by their reporting branch.
task: Use a WITH RECURSIVE CTE to find every direct and indirect report of employee_id = 10, at any depth. Do not include employee 10 or employees in unrelated reporting trees.
Set depth to 1 for direct reports, 2 for employees reporting to a direct report, and so on.

For each employee, branch_id must identify the direct report of employee 10 through whom that employee reports. For a direct report, branch_id equals their own employee_id; all descendants inherit that branch_id.
Display exactly employee_id, employee_name, manager_id, depth and branch_id. Sort by depth ascending, branch_id ascending, then employee_id ascending. Do not hardcode report IDs or a maximum depth.
questions.hint: The anchor query selects employees whose manager_id is 10. In the recursive member, join employees to the previous level by manager_id = employee_id, increment depth, and carry forward branch_id.
questions.solution:
WITH RECURSIVE reporting_tree AS (
    SELECT employee_id, employee_name, manager_id,
           1 AS depth, employee_id AS branch_id
    FROM employees
    WHERE manager_id = 10
    UNION ALL
    SELECT e.employee_id, e.employee_name, e.manager_id,
           r.depth + 1, r.branch_id
    FROM employees AS e
    JOIN reporting_tree AS r ON e.manager_id = r.employee_id
)
SELECT employee_id, employee_name, manager_id, depth, branch_id
FROM reporting_tree
ORDER BY depth, branch_id, employee_id;
steps: The anchor query finds Ben (11) and Charu (12) because their manager_id is 10. Give each depth 1 and their own ID as branch_id.
The first recursive iteration finds Dev (13) and Esha (14) reporting to Ben, and Gopal (16) reporting to Charu. Give them depth 2 and inherited branch IDs 11, 11 and 12.
The next iteration finds Farah (15) under Dev and Hana (17) under Gopal. Both have depth 3; their branch IDs are still 11 and 12.
Neither Farah nor Hana has a report, so the next iteration returns no rows and recursion stops. The unrelated tree starting at Ishan (20) never enters the anchor or recursion.
UNION ALL combines the anchor and every recursive level. The final ORDER BY produces the seven rows in depth, branch and ID order.
